title: Janardhan Bhat vs Dattatraya G. Hedge (Air 2008 Scw 788); ... on 18 September, 2021
full_text: Janardhan Bhat vs Dattatraya G. Hedge (Air 2008 Scw 788); ... on 18 September, 2021 IN THE COURT OF METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE (NI-03), CENTRAL, TIS HAZARI COURTS, DELHI Presided over by: Ms. Isha Singh Case no. : 4563/2017 Unique Case ID no. : DLCT020071052017 In the matter of : M/s Mahendru Tex Fab 6187, Gali no. 2&3, Basement, Block no. 1, Dev Nagar, Karol Bagh, New Delhi- 110005 ............ COMPLAINANT Versus Rahul Kumar Flat no. 44, Ground Floor, Pocket no.1, Ner Murliwala Sweets, Paschim Puri, Delhi Also At M/s Balaji Garments, Shop H-16/52, Gali no. 4, Tank Road, Karol Bagh, New Delhi-110005 ............ACCUSED 1. Name of the Complainant : M/S Mahendru Tex Fab 2. Name of the Accused : Rahul Kumar 3. Offence complained of or proved : Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 4. Plea of the Accused : Not Guilty 5. Date of Filing : 20.03.2017 6. Date of Reserving Order : 10.09.2021 7. Date of Pronouncement : 18.09.2021 8. Final Order : CONVICTED BRIEF STATEMENT OF REASONS OF DECISION CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 1 of 20 FACTUAL MATRIX 1. The present complaint has been filed by M/S Mahendru Tex Fab (hereinafter "complainant") against Mr. Rahul Kumar (hereinafter "accused") under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter " NI Act "). 2. The substance of allegations, as contained in the complaint, are as follows: (a) That the complainant is a reputed sole trading business under the proprietorship of Mr. Mahendra Chawla. Accused, being the proprietor of M/s Balaji Garments, was in the business of purchasing clothing items from the complainant. On 11.01.2017, the accused had purchased some shirts from the complainant and in lieu of the same, the complainant firm has issued a retail/credit memo bearing no. 5578 amounting to Rs. 18,75,132/-. The accused duly acknowledged the receipt of goods on the credit memo itself. At that time, the accused promised to pay the aforesaid amount in one or two installments and requested for some time. (b) It is further the case of the complainant that after some time, the accused came to the shop of the complainant in Karol Bagh and in discharge of his legal liability issued a cheque bearing no.116789 dated 30.01.2017 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132/- drawn on Axis Bank, Patel Nagar (E), New Delhi-110008 in the name of the complainant with an assurance that the same shall be encashed on its presentation. (c) The aforesaid cheque was presented by the complainant for payment through its banker -HDFC Bank, Karol Bagh, New Delhi for its encashment, however the same was returned as dishonoured vide cheque returning memo dated 03.02.2017 with the remarks "funds insufficient". Thereafter, the complainant sent a legal notice dated 16.02.2017 by way of registered AD and speed post. It is the case of the complainant that despite service/deemed service of legal notice dated 17.09.2015, the accused failed to repay the cheque amount within the stipulated period and hence, the present complaint was filed on 20.03.2017 under section 138 of the NI Act. APPEARANCE OF THE ACCUSED 3. Pre-summoning evidence was led by the complainant and upon finding a prima facie case against the accused, he was summoned to face trial vide order dated 03.08.2017, and after his appearance, notice of accusation under Sec. 251, The Code of Criminal CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 2 of 20 Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter " CrPC ") was served upon him on 10.01.2019 to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. After perusal of the cheque, the accused stated that the cheque in question was issued to the complainant as a blank signed security cheque in the course of business. The accused admitted his signatures on the cheque in question, but he denied the receipt of legal notice and denied having any outstanding liability towards the complainant. At the time of framing of notice under Sec. 251 CrPC, the accused took the following plea of defence: "I had issued blank signed security cheque to the complainant during the time when I used to do business with the complainant. The cheque in question was a security cheque which has been misused by the complainant. I stopped doing business with the complainant as he was selling goods at a higher rate and I had requested the complainant to return my security cheque to which the complainant told me that when he find the said cheque, then he will return to me. I came to know that my cheque has been misused when I received from the court." 4. Considering the plea of defence raised and in view of the application filed by the accused under Sec.145(2) , NI Act, accused was allowed the opportunity under Sec. 145(2) NI Act, to cross-examine the complainant vide order dated 10.01.2019. 5. During the course of trial, the complainant led the following oral and documentary evidence in order to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt: Oral Evidence CW1 Mahendra Chawla (Proprietor of the complainant firm) Documentary Evidence Ex. CW 1/A Credit memo bearing no. 5578 dated 11.01.2017 in the name of M/s Balaji Garments amounting to Rs. 18,75,132/- Ex. CW 1/B Cheque in question bearing no. 116789 dated 30.01.2017 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132/- Ex. CW 1/C Return Memo dated 03.02.2017 Ex. CW 1/D Legal Demand Notice dated CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 3 of 20 16.02.2017 Ex. CW 1/E Postal Receipts for legal demand notice Ex. CW 1/F Internet generated tracking report Ex. CW 1/D1 (OSR) Income Tax Return (ITR) of the complainant firm for the Financial year 2016-17 Ex. CW 1/D1X (colly) Account statement/ledger of the complainant firm for the financial year 01.04.2016 to 31.03.2017 Ex. CW 1/D1Y Certificate under Sec. 65B, IEA. Once the aforesaid evidence was led, thereafter cross-examination was closed vide a separate statement of the complainant recorded to that effect. STATEMENT OF THE ACCUSED 6. After the completion of complainant evidence and before the start of defence evidence, in order to enable the accused to personally explain the circumstances appearing in evidence against him, his statement under Sec. 313 , CrPC was recorded without oath. In his statement under Sec. 313 CrPC, the accused denied the signature on Ex. CW1/A and denied having purchased goods from the complainant, as alleged in the complaint and as represented in the invoice. He reiterated himself by saying that the cheque in question was issued as a blank signed security cheque to the complainant. As regards the legal demand notice, he denied the receipt thereof. 7. Pursuant thereto, the accused did not enter the witness box himself or led any other evidence. 8. Thereafter, final arguments were heard in the present case, I have heard the learned counsels on both sides and given my thoughtful consideration to the material appearing on record. ARGUMENTS 9. It has been argued by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant that all ingredients of Sec. 138 NI Act, have been fulfilled in the present case and that the complainant has duly CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 4 of 20 proved his case. It was argued that accused admitted his signatures on the cheque. He argued that the credit memo Ex.CW1/A has been duly acknowledged by the accused by signing on the same. Further, he argued that the name of the firm of the accused has been duly reflected in the list of sundry debtors under the audited balance sheet of the complainant firm as on 31 March 2017, filed as an annexure to the tax audit report in Form No.3CD along with the Income Tax Return of the complainant firm which is Ex. CW1/D1. He pointed out that the entry against the name of the firm of the accused under the head of sundry debtors is in the sum of Rs.18,75,132/- which tallies with the cheque amount. He further argued that the debt recoverable under the cheque in question is duly corroborated by the ledger account statement for the complainant firm for the year 2016-17 which is Ex. CW1/D1X. The sales entry of date 11.01.2017 in the ledger account maintained by the complainant for the accounts of the firm of the accused tallies with the sale of the goods to the firm of the accused in the sum of Rs.18,75,132/- on 11.01.2017, and thereafter the return of the cheque is also corroborated vide entry dated 03.02.2017. It was argued that accused failed to raise the probable defence to disprove the case of complainant and to rebut the presumptions under Section 118 and Section 139 NI Act. Ld. Counsel for the complainant relied upon Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar (2019) 4 SCC 197; V.S. Yadav v. Reena 2010 DLT 561; Suresh Chand Goyal v. Amit Singhal 2015 LawSuit (Del) 2361; Bharath Barrel and Drum Manufacturing Company v. Amin Chand Pyarelal (1999) 3 SCC 35; Rohitbhai Jivanlal Patel v. State of Gujarat (2019) 18 SCC 106; M/s Kalamani Tex & Anr. V. P. Balasubramanium Crl. Appeal No. 123 of 2021 (SC); C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed, (2007) 6 SCC 555. As such, it is prayed that the accused be punished for the said offence. 10. Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the accused has argued that the complainant has failed to establish his case beyond reasonable doubt. The Counsel for the accused has argued that the cheque in question was issued by way of security to the complainant in the course of business with him, which has been misused by him. He has argued that the credit memo Ex. CW1/A is fabricated by the complainant. As regards the Income Tax Return of the complainant firm Ex. CW1/D1(OSR) and the ledger account filed by the complainant firm for the year 2016-17 Ex. CW1/D1X, the counsel argued that the same should not be relied upon as complainant despite not being the author of such documents, has brought these documents on record. He further argued that the ledger CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 5 of 20 has been fabricated as the same is silent as to the cash transactions of the firm of the accused with that of the complainant prior to the transaction in question, whereas for other businesses, cash transactions have been duly reflected in the ledger account maintained by the complainant firm. He argued that the credit memo is silent as to the transportation details or the delivery of the alleged goods, for which reason its credibility is doubtful. He has contended that the service of the legal notice was manipulated and since the notice was never served upon the accused, therefore ingredients of Sec.138 , NI Act are not made out. He has pointed out inconsistencies in the case of the complainant to the extent that the complainant in his cross-examination stated that the cheque was handed over to him at the time of delivery of goods and drawing of the credit memo dated 11.01.2017 whereas in his evidence by way of affidavit at pre summoning stage, the complainant has stated that the cheque was handed over at a time later than the delivery of goods. He has argued that the complainant ought to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt for securing conviction in the present case and the case of the complainant must stand on its own legs. In order to buttress his submissions, ld. Counsel for the accused has relied upon Krishna Janardhan Bhat versus Dattatraya G. Hedge (AIR 2008 SCW 788); Basalingappa vs. Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418 and Kulvinder Singh v. Kafeel Ahmad 2014 (2) JCC (NI) 100; K. Prakashan v. PK Surenderam decided on 10 October 2007 (SC); Nagasubramaniam v. M/s Hope Knitting Home decided on 11 March 2004 in Crl A. No. 22/1998 and Vipul Kumar Gupta v. Vipin Gupta decided on 24.08.2021 in Crl. No. 461/2011 (Del HC). As such, it is prayed that the accused be acquitted. INGREDIENTS OF THE OFFENCE 11. Before dwelling into the facts of the present case, it would be apposite to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both sides. In order to establish the offence under Section 138 of NI Act, the prosecution must fulfil all the essential ingredients of the offence. Perusal of the bare provision reveals the following necessary ingredients of the offence: - First Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by a person on an account maintained by him for payment of money and the same is presented for payment within a period of 3 months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity; CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 6 of 20 Second Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by the drawer for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability; Third Ingredient: The cheque was returned unpaid by the bank due to either insufficiency of funds in the account to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account on an agreement made with that bank; Fourth Ingredient: A demand of the said amount has been made by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque by a notice in writing given to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information of the dishonour of cheque from the bank; Fifth Ingredient: The drawer fails to make payment of the said amount of money within fifteen days from the date of receipt of notice. 12. The accused can only be held guilty of the offence under Section 138 NI Act if the above-mentioned ingredients are proved by the complainant co-extensively. Additionally, the conditions stipulated under Section 142 NI Act have to be fulfilled. 13. Notably, the first, third, fourth and fifth ingredient have been duly proved without there being any real controversy regarding the same. (a) The complainant has proved the original cheque, Ex. CW1/B, which the accused has not disputed as being drawn on the account of the accused. It is not disputed that the cheque in question was presented within its validity period. (b) The cheque in question was returned unpaid vide return memos dated 03.02.2017 which is Ex. CW1/C due to the reason, "Funds Insufficient". (c) The complainant has proved on record the legal demand notice vide Ex. CW1/D dated 16.02.2017, postal receipts vide Ex. CW1/E, internet generated tracking report Ex. CW 1/F to prove the fact of sending legal notice. However, in the notice under Sec.251 , CrPC the accused has asserted that the address on the legal notice is wrong and has denied the receipt of legal notice. He has contended that the service of the legal notice was manipulated. He contended that the complainant, in his evidence by way of affidavit Ex. CW1/1 stated that legal notice was served upon both addresses of the accused for which he had tendered the postal receipt which is Ex. CW1/E. However, it is the case of the accused that the address CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 7 of 20 mentioned upon the legal notice Ex.CW1/D was only one of the addresses of the accused, which was also wrong. He has further contended that as per the tracking report on record which is Ex. CW1/F, the item was undelivered and was returned to the complainant, therefore the ingredients of Section 138 are not made out since the legal demand notice was never served upon the accused within the statutory period under the Act. Ld. Counsel for the accused has placed reliance on the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Madras in the case of Nagasubramaniam v. M/s Hope Knitting Home decided on 11 March 2004 in Crl A. No. 22/1998. This assertion, cannot help the accused in escaping liability under section 138 NI Act, especially keeping in mind that the summons issued by the court were served on the accused at the same address as mentioned in the legal notice. It has been settled by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the judgement reported as, C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed, (2007) 6 SCC 555 that an accused who claims that he did not receive the legal notice, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court, make payment of the cheque amount, and an accused who does not make such payment cannot contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. 14. On analysis of the facts and legal position stated above, the Court finds the parties to be at variance on the primary issue i.e. whether the cheque in question were issued in favour of the complainant in order to discharge the legal liability of the accused which forms the second ingredient in the Section 138 , NI Act. 15. As regards the second ingredient, it has to be proved that the cheques in question were drawn by the drawer for discharging a legally enforceable debt. In the present case, the signatures of the accused on the cheques in question are not denied. Under the NI Act , once the accused admits his signatures on the cheque, certain presumptions are drawn, which result in shifting of onus. Section 118(a) of the NI Act lays down the presumption that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration. The second presumption is contained under Section 139 of NI Act. The provision lays down the presumption that the holder of the cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or part, of any debt or other liability. The combined effect of these two provisions is a presumption that the cheque was drawn for consideration and given by the accused for the discharge of debt or other liability. Both the sections use the word CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 8 of 20 "shall", which makes raising the presumption imperative for the court, once the foundational facts required to raise the presumption are proved {Reliance is placed upon Hiten P. Dalal vs. Bratindranath Banerjee (2001) 6 SCC 16}. 16. Further, it has been held by a three-judge bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441 that the presumption contemplated under Section 139 of NI Act includes the presumption of existence of a legally enforceable debt. Once the presumption is raised, it is for the accused to rebut the same by establishing a probable defence. The principles pertaining to the presumptions and the onus of proof were recently summarized by the Hon'ble Apex Court in Basalingappa vs. Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418 as under: "25. We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in the above cases on Section 118(a) and 139 , we now summarise the principles enumerated by this Court in the following manner: 25.1. Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of theAct mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. 25.2. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. 25.3. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. 25.4. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. 25.5. It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence." CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 9 of 20 17. The presumptions raised under Section 118(b) and Section 139 are rebuttable presumptions. A reverse onus is cast on the accused, who has to establish a probable defence on the standard of preponderance of probabilities to prove that either there was no legally enforceable debt or other liability. In the present case, ld. counsel for the accused has raised many defences to rebut the presumption, which are discussed hereinbelow: THAT THE CHEQUE IN QUESTION WAS ISSUED AS SECURITY 18. In the notice under Sec. 251 CrPC, the accused has raised the plea that the cheque in question was issued as a blank signed security cheque to the complainant at the time when he used to have business transactions with the complainant. The defence of the accused is pivoted around the contention that the complainant misused the cheques that the accused had given to him earlier at the time of doing business with him. The accused further states, in the notice framed under Sec. 251 CrPC, that he stopped dealing with the complainant as the latter started selling him goods at higher rates and due to this abrupt end to the business, the security cheques of the accused were never returned to him and instead were misused. During the cross-examination of the complainant, suggestions have been put to the complainant to the effect that name, amount (numerically and alphabetically) were filled by the complainant, which he has denied. 19. Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the complainant has relied upon the judgement of Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar (2019) 4 SCC 197 to contend that even a blank signed cheque leaf, voluntarily signed and handed over by the accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act, in the absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt. 20. The defence of the accused is nothing more than a bald assertion. At nowhere has the accused produced anything on record to back this claim. If the cheque in question had indeed been misused by the complainant and not returned despite repeated requests, then the accused could have informed the bank as regards the same and could have stopped payment for the cheque in question, however the accused has chosen not to do the same. The accused did not even examine himself and subject himself to cross- CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 10 of 20 examination on this point. Without any of these, the court is not inclined to accept this averment of the accused. THAT INCOME TAX RETURN PRODUCED BY THE COMPLAINANT CANNOT BE RELIED UPON 21. Upon being questioned by the counsel for the accused, as to whether any account statement of the complainant firm for the year 2016-17 has been placed on record, the complainant, at the stage of cross-examination, filed the Income Tax Return (ITR) of the complainant firm for the Financial year 2016-17 which is Ex. CW1/D1(OSR); account statement/ledger of the complainant firm for the financial year 01.04.2016 to 31.03.2017 which is Ex. CW1/D1X and Certificate under Sec.65B, IEA for the aforesaid documents which is Ex. CW1/D1Y. 22. The ITR of Financial year 2016-17 which is Ex. CW1/D1(OSR) was objected to by the Ld. Counsel for the accused for its mode of proof. The Ld. Counsel for the accused contended that the complainant was not the author of the ITR Documents, so therefore he cannot prove the same and that the proper course is to summon the Income-tax Officer, who produced the documents, or a subordinate of his to prove the same. 23. It is settled by the Andhra Pradesh High Court in the judgement of Pentakota Surya Appa Rao And Ors. vs Pentakota Seethayamma And Ors. 1976 103 ITR 222 AP, that income tax returns are public documents within the meaning of Section 74 , since they are documents forming the acts of public officers who discharge executive functions by imposing and collecting tax, so therefore when originals of public documents are produced, they require no further proof. Even the Madras High court in the case of Rama Rao vs Venkataramayya 1940 8 ITR 450 Mad held that a profit and loss statement and a statement showing the details of net income, filed by an assessee in support of his return of income furnished under Section 22 of the Indian Income-tax Act, are public documents with reference to Section 74 of the Evidence Act of which certified copies would be admissible under Section 65 (e) of Evidence Act. 24. In view of the settled law, the objection by the accused does not hold water and deserves dismissal. The ITR documents are public documents within the meaning of CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 11 of 20 Section 74 , Indian Evidence Act and as such require no further proof. Thus, there is no mandate that the ITR shall only be taken into consideration after it has been summoned and an official from the income tax department is called to prove the same. No matter who produces it, it is good evidence of the original, since the ITR is a public document within the meaning of Section 74 , IEA. 25. In the present case, the complainant has filed internet generated copy of the Indian Income Tax Return Acknowledgment for the financial year 2016-2017 along with Form no. 3CB, i.e., tax audit report furnished by the Chartered Accountant of the complainant firm for the financial year 2016-2017, and Form No. 3CD containing statements of the particulars which are required to be furnished under Section 44AB of the Income Tax Act and also audited balance sheet, trading and profit & loss account statement et al filed by the chartered accountant as annexure to the Form no. 3CD. In addition to these, the complainant has also filed Certificate under Sec.65B, IEA which is Ex. CW1/D1Y certifying that the computer-generated copies of the ITR for the financial year 2016-17 are true and have not been tampered at all. 26. The case of the complainant is that the accused purchased goods on credit worth Rs.18,75,132/- from the complainant and thereafter, he defaulted payment. To prove the same, the complainant has brought on record Form No. 3CD containing statements of the particulars which are required to be furnished under Section 44AB of the Income Tax Act and along-with he has brought the audited balance sheet on record for the complainant firm as on 31 March 2017 which also bears the stamp of the chartered accountant and is at page 16 of Ex. CW1/D1(OSR). A figure of Rs. 10120126.00 appears against the entry of sundry debtor in the audited balance sheet annexed to Form no.3CD filed by the complainant firm with the Income Tax Department. The audited balance sheet states that the sundry debtors have been furnished as per list attached. The list of sundry debtors as on 31 March 2017 is appended to the audited balance sheet and shows a debt of Rs.18,75,132 against the entry of M/s Balaji Garment, which is the proprietorship of the accused. This debt of Rs. 18,75,132 shown against the entry of M/s Balaji Garment as on 31 March 2017 tallies with the cheque amount in question. CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 12 of 20 27. By way of the ITR of the complainant firm which is Ex. CW1/D1(OSR), and particularly the audited balance sheet and the list of sundry debtors, the complainant has corroborated his evidence that an amount of Rs.18,75,132 stood as a debt due from the accused at the end of the financial year, which was duly reflected in the list of sundry debtors attached to the audited balance sheet filed by the complainant firm as annexure to Form No. 3CD. 28. Ld. Counsel for the accused has challenged the ITR on two grounds: firstly, that the list of sundry debtors does not mention the cheque number in question along with the figure of Rs.1875132 shown against the entry of M/s Balaji Garments; secondly, the ITR is a fabricated document which was created only after the complainant was asked for the same during the course of cross-examination and did not file it along with the pre-summoning evidence. 29. These arguments of the Ld. Counsel of the accused do not inspire confidence of the court. There is no requirement to mention the cheque number against the entry of Rs.18,75,132/- shown as debt due from M/s Balaji Garments in the list of sundry debtors of the complainant firm as on 31 March 2017. As far as the contention that the ITR furnished by the complainant is fabricated, the same is insufficiently challenged. The accused has not led any evidence to prove that the ITR including the audited balance sheets of the complainant firm for the year 2017-18 are forged or fabricated. To prove his case, the accused could have summoned officials from the Income Tax department to prove that the ITR filed by the complainant is tampered with and fabricated or he could have led evidence to show that the debt stood paid as on 31 March 2017, but he has chosen not to act either way. It is no denying that, submission of income tax return constitutes the fulfilment of several parameters, tallying of the total assets and liabilities of the firm, calculation of the income assessable to tax and in the absence of any independent evidence on record, the Income tax return cannot be rejected, especially when it corroborates the case of the complainant. The audited balance sheet is relevant both as corroborating the evidence of the complainant itself and as rebutting the contention that the income tax return and ledger account was fabricated and created only during trial, upon being asked for the same. CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 13 of 20 30. Thus, in the absence of independent evidence on record, the contention of the accused that the ITR of the complainant firm has been fabricated, does not inspire confidence of the court and the same is rejected. THAT THE LEDGER ACCOUNT OF THE COMPLAINANT FIRM IS FABRICATED AND CANNOT BE RELIED UPON 31. Upon being questioned by the counsel for the accused, as to whether any account statement of the complainant firm for the year 2016-17 has been placed on record, the complainant, at the stage of cross-examination, filed the account statement/ledger account of the complainant firm for the financial year 01.04.2016 to 31.03.2017 which is Ex. CW1/D1X. 32. The ledger book of the complainant firm which is Ex. CW1/D1X was objected to by the Ld. Counsel for the accused for its mode of proof. The Ld. Counsel for the accused contended that the complainant was not the author of the ledger account/account statement of the complainant firm, so therefore he cannot prove the same and that the proper course is to summon the accountant who prepared the ledger, to prove the same. He further contended that the complainant, during his cross-examination has admitted that the ledger account Ex.CW1/D1X has been prepared by his accountant, but the same is not certified by the accountant, therefore the same cannot be relied upon. 33. The objection raised by the counsel for the accused is a technical objection which does not affect the purpose, import or relevancy of the document under consideration. It is worth observing that the ledger account which is Ex. CW1/D1X bears the signature of the complainant/proprietor on each page. In addition to this, the complainant has filed Certificate under Sec.65B, IEA which is Ex. CW1/D1Y certifying that the ledger account for the complainant firm for the financial year 2016- 17 is true and has not been tampered at all. It cannot be said that copy of the ledger account uncertified by the accountant, cannot be tendered in evidence by the proprietor of the business. Complainant being the proprietor of the firm is in control and possession of account statements, ledger accounts of the firm and can produce the same, after assuming full responsibility of the veracity of the same. It is immaterial, as to who, whether the complainant or his accountant produces the ledger account. In the present case, the accountant was not cited as witness, however the complainant upon being questioned, during his cross-examination, produced the account CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 14 of 20 statement/ledger account of the complainant firm to discharge his onus and prove the liability of the accused. Mere objection as to production of a document by a person shall not water down the purpose, import or relevancy of the document under consideration. 34. Further, the counsel for the accused has contended that the ledger account is fabricated and has only been created at a later date, to fill in the lacunae in the case of the complainant. Ld. Counsel for the accused contended that despite the complainant's admission in his cross-examination that there were cash transactions between the parties prior to the transaction in question, the same was not reflected in the ledger account balance. Ld. Counsel highlighted that cash entries for other firms/individuals were duly reflected in the ledger account, however there was no cash entry for the firm of the accused, despite the fact that even complainant admitted having had cash transactions with the accused. He pointed out first entry on page 3 of Ex. CW1/D1X, under the ledger account for "A.B. Enterprises-Puri" being "cash received" in the sum of Rs.19,980 dated 15.02.2017. Ld. Counsel for accused pointed out that if cash entries of other firms were being recorded, then why the same was not done for M/s Balaji Garments. Ld. Counsel for the accused, on the basis of above arguments contended that the complainant has prepared incorrect ledger account pertaining to the accused and same should not be relied upon. 35. Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the complainant contended that as per the accounting rules, the ledger account is maintained for only such transactions where the payment is deferred by the buyer. He further submitted that entries in cash which are being reflected for other businesses/firms are cash payments received against the goods sold to those businesses at an earlier date on credit, where the payment was deferred at request. Thereafter, he submitted that as and when payment in cash or by way of cheque is received from the buyer, the same is added to the account of the buyer and accordingly, the account of the buyer is closed. 36. Perusal of the ledger account shows that under the head of Balaji Garments, there are three entries which are duly reflected. First entry dated 11.01.2017 is a sales entry against bill no. 5578 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132. Second entry dated 02.02.2017 is the receipt of cheque bearing no. 116789 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132. Third entry dated CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 15 of 20 03.02.2017 signifies the return of cheque bearing no. 116789 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132. 37. The complainant, during his cross-examination (dated 19.07.2019), has admitted that prior to the transaction in question, the accused once or twice had purchased the goods from the complainant in cash/cheque. Thereafter, when the complainant was confronted with Ex.CW1/D1X during his cross-examination (dated 16.08.2019) and was asked as to how many transactions existed between the complainant and accused during the period 01.04.2016 and 31.03.2017, the complainant stated that only one transaction on credit which is duly reflected in Ex.CW1/D1X was conducted between the parties. He further stated that there may have been other transactions with the accused, which he cannot specifically recall, however for such cash transactions, cash memos must have been issued which are not reflected in Ex.CW1/D1X. Whereas, on the contrary, in his cross-examination (dated 27.09.2019), the complainant stated that for the period prior to 01.07.2017, even on receipt of payment in cash, entry used to be reflected in the ledger balance. 38. It is the case of the accused that he had dealt in cash transactions prior to the transaction in question with the complainant and since those transactions are not featured in the ledger account maintained for his firm with the complainant, therefore the ledger is false and fabricated. This court is unable to agree with the accused. Had it been the case of the accused that he has made part or full payment in cash to the complainant as regards the transaction in question and that net amount due was lesser than claimed and despite the same, no receipt was generated or no entry was reflected in the ledger, then there would have arisen a case of false and fabricated ledger. That is to say, if the accused had alleged multiple entries after the transaction in question which would have resulted in setting off of the amount due but the benefit of set off was not given by the complainant, then it could be said that ledger was incorrectly fabricated. In the present set of facts, whether or not cash transactions between the complainant and the accused prior to the present transaction are reflected in the ledger account or not, will have no bearing on the transaction in question. 39. In the existing facts and circumstances, first entry in the ledger account under the head of M/s Balaji Garments dated 11.01.2017 is a sales entry against bill no. 5578 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132 which is duly corroborated by Ex.CW1/1 Credit invoice no. CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 16 of 20 5578 dated 11.01.2017 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132 drawn upon M/s Balaji Garments, which bears the acknowledgement of the accused. Second entry dated 02.02.2017 denoting the receipt of cheque bearing no. 116789 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132 and third entry dated 03.02.2017 denoting the return of cheque bearing no. 116789 in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132 is duly corroborated by the cheque in question Ex.CW1/2 and return memo dated 03.02.2017 bearing remarks "funds insufficient" which is Ex. CW1/3. 40. Thus, the defence of the accused that the ledger is fabricated and must not be relied upon, does not inspire confidence of the court. THAT THE CREDIT MEMO IS FABRICATED 41. In the statement recorded under Sec.313 CrPC, the accused has denied his signatures on the credit memo Ex. CW1/A and has denied purchasing any goods from the complainant as alleged in the complaint or detailed in the credit memo. Ld. Counsel for the accused has contended that the credit memo Ex.CW1/A is fabricated by the complainant for the purposes of the present case. During the cross-examination of the complainant, suggestions were put to him as to the credit memo Ex.CW1/A being silent on the transportation details. It has also been contended on behalf of the accused that no delivery note has been filed by the complainant denoting the delivery of items to the accused. In addition to that, it has been argued that the Ex.CW1/A is not a "pakka" receipt and it has been assailed on the ground that no address of the accused has been mentioned upon the credit invoice. The counsel for the complainant, at the stage of final arguments, argued that Ex.CW1/A is a handwritten credit memo which is devoid of details as to broker, transportation, GST number, date of receipt of goods, therefore the same should not be relied upon. He further contended that although complainant had admitted during his cross-examination that the cheque in question was handed over to him on the same day itself when the delivery of goods was taken by the accused, however the details of the cheque in question so handed over to the complainant do not find a mention upon the credit memo Ex.CW1/A. He also argued that VAT number of the complainant firm is not mentioned upon the credit memo Ex.CW1/A. He also contended that the signatures on the cheque in question Ex. CW1/B and those on the credit memo Ex.CW1/A are not the same, and hence signatures on the credit memo Ex.CW1/A are denied by the accused. CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 17 of 20 42. Ld. Counsel for the complainant has contended that credit memo Ex.CW1/1 is a "pakka receipt" since the same entry of sales for the amount of Rs.18,75,132 dated 11.01.2017 finds mention in the ledger account Ex. CW1/D1X. He further contended that the accused has not led any evidence to disprove the credit memo Ex.CW1/1. As regards the want of transportation details on the credit memo, counsel for the complainant contended that the same is managed by the purchasing party itself and even in the present case, the accused managed the transportation on his own. Ld. Counsel thus contended that all the defences taken by the accused are bare denials of existence of the transaction in question, without having led any evidence to disprove the same. He has relied upon the judgement of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of V.S. Yadav v. Reena 2010 DLT 561 which has been reiterated in Suresh Chand Goyal v. Amit Singhal 2015 LawSuit (Del) 2361 where it has been held that statement of the accused under Section 281 CrPC or under Section 313 CrPC is not the evidence of the accused and it cannot be read as part of evidence. Where the accused does not examine himself as a witness, his statement under Section 281 or 313 CrPC cannot be read as evidence and it has to be looked into only as an explanation of the incriminating circumstances and not as evidence. 43. In the existing facts and circumstances, this court finds force in the arguments of the counsel for the complainant. Apart from denying the factum of Credit memo and the signatures thereon in the statement recorded under Section 313 CrPC, the accused has not led any independent evidence to assail the credit memo. On the other hand, the total amount of the goods purchased on credit by the accused and reflected so in the credit invoice memo in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132 stands duly corroborated by Income tax return and audited balance sheet of the complainant firm for the year 2016-17 Ex. CW1/D1(OSR) which shows a record entry of Rs. 18,75,132 against the name of the firm of the accused, M/s Balaji Garments maintained under the head of under sundry debtors as on 31.03.2017. Further, the credit invoice memo in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132 drawn upon the accused for purchase of goods by the accused on 11.01.2017 is also corroborated by an entry in the sum of Rs. 18,75,132 of even date under the head "M/s Balaji Garments" maintained in the ledger account statement of the complainant firm for the year 2016-17 which is Ex. CW1/D1X. The contention of fabrication of the credit memo stands duly rebutted by the evidence in the form of ITR, audited balance sheet and ledger account statement brought on record by the CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 18 of 20 complainant as the argument of fabrication becomes inconsistent with the existence of these statements and accounts already maintained by the complainant in the past. 44. Ld. Counsel for the accused further contended that after the accused had denied his signatures on the credit memo Ex.CW1/A, the complainant should have examined handwriting expert for proving otherwise or should have called the accused as a witness for proving the signatures on credit memo Ex.CW1/A. He has further contended that the complainant has also failed to file an application for sending the credit memo Ex. CW 1/A to the Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) for proving the signatures of the accused on the credit memo or for comparison of those with that on the cheque in question. Ld. Counsel further contended that the complainant did not call any employee of his firm to prove the supply of goods to the accused as alleged in the complaint. 45. Per contra, the counsel for the complainant has contended that Section 139 , NI Act is a reverse onus clause where the accused ought to disprove the presumption raised against him by showing cogent and convincing evidence. In this regard, he has relied upon Bharath Barrel and Drum Manufacturing Company v. Amin Chand Pyarelal (1999) 3 SCC 35. The Ld. Counsel placed reliance upon Section 102 , Indian Evidence Act to contend that onus of proof lies upon the accused, in a situation where presumptions already stand in favour of the complainant and against the accused. 46. It is a settled law that Presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act, is in the nature of a 'rebuttable' presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested, therefore Section 139 of the N.I. Act is an example of a reverse onus clause (Rangappa v. Sri Mohan, 2010 (11) SCC 441). In the given set of facts and circumstances, it was upon the accused to have brought evidence on record to the effect that signatures on the credit memo Ex. CW1/A were not his. To prove the same, the accused could have gotten examined a private handwriting expert but he has chosen not to. Also neither has the accused filed any application for sending the credit memo Ex. CW 1/A to the Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) for proving that signatures on the credit memo Ex. CW1/A were not actually not his own and were forged. Thus, the credit memo Ex. CC No. 4563/17 Mahendru Tex Fab v. Rahul Kumar Page 19 of 20 CW1/A remains insufficiently challenged by the accused and the contention of the accused that the credit memo Ex. CW1/A was fabricated, cannot be accepted. 47. Hence, in view of the discussion in the foregoing paragraphs, the inevitable conclusion is that the accused has failed to rebut the onus put on him by virtue of the presump- tions enshrined in Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act. Therefore, the second ingredient also stands proved against the accused. CONCLUSION 48. To recapitulate the above discussion, the complainant has been successful in establishing his case beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had issued the cheque in question in discharge of his legally enforceable liability. The presumptions under Section 118 and Section 139 of NI Act were drawn against the accused. The accused has failed to rebut the said presumption by raising a probable defence. The defence of the accused that the complainant misused the cheque in question and there was no legal liability is not proved, even on the standard of preponderance of probabilities. 49. Resultantly, the complaint of the complainant M/S Mahendru Tex Fab is allowed and the accused Mr. Rahul Kumar is hereby convicted of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Let the convict be heard separately on quantum of sentence. 50. A copy of this judgment be given free of cost to the convict.
